strengths: The MDP formulation is clean and well-motivated: casting the prompt-refinement policy's state as (x_t, c_t, q, t) and the action as the refined prompt c_{t-1} yields a genuinely useful structural analogy to weight-level diffusion RL (Table 1, Fig. 3), which is a novel and conceptually satisfying framing rather than a mere repackaging of prior prompt-tuning work.

The core technical idea—feeding the denoised latent estimate x̂_t (Eq. 9) back to the MLLM policy so that refinement is conditioned on the evolving visual state—is a meaningful departure from existing feed-forward prompt-refinement methods that apply a single refined prompt across the whole trajectory (Mañas et al., Hao et al., Wu et al.).

Experiments are broad and cover the four claimed properties: single-reward alignment (Table 2, SD1.5 and SDXL), composite-reward alignment (Table 3, SDXL-turbo with GenEval), orthogonality by layering PromptLoop on DDPO/ReFL/NPNet/Diffusion-DPO, and generalization to unseen backbones. The ablation in Table 4 cleanly isolates each component (policy alone hurts, GRPO helps, multi-step helps, visual feedback helps most).

The sparse-refinement strategy (Sec. 3.3, R ⊆ {1,…,T}) is a practical and clearly motivated engineering choice that makes the method tractable without co-residing a large MLLM with the diffusion backbone at every step.

The observation that visual feedback is not required at inference time once the policy has learned the environment dynamics—and the resulting efficiency/compatibility with existing generation pipelines—is a genuinely useful practical finding.
The prompt-evolution analysis (Table 5, Appendix D.1) is insightful and interpretable, and the emergent resemblance to CFG scheduling behavior is a nice, well-argued qualitative result.
Implementation details (Sec. C.1, Algorithms 1–2) are sufficiently specified (Qwen2.5-VL-3B policy, LoRA rank 16, GRPO group size 8, β values, bf16, 4×A100) to support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Evaluation circularity: the headline metric is ImageReward, which is also the training reward for the single-reward setting. Although HPSv2, Aesthetics, and VLLM score are reported, the VLLM-score evaluator uses Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct—the same base model as the policy—which introduces a plausible self-preference bias in that metric. A cleaner evaluation with an independent reward/evaluator would strengthen the alignment claims.

The RePrompt baseline is not the original method but a re-implementation obtained by stripping visual feedback and multi-turn refinement from PromptLoop (Sec. C.4). Similarly, the orthogonality experiments apply PromptLoop on top of other methods, which structurally favors PromptLoop. The 'orthogonality/generalization' story would be more convincing with the actual released RePrompt checkpoints, as is done for DDPO/ReFL/Diffusion-DPO/NPNet.

The reward-hacking / over-optimization claim (abstract, Sec. 4.2) is supported mainly by qualitative comparison (Fig. 4) and a subjective assertion that ReFL 'resembl[es] reward hacking from a human perspective.' There is no quantitative anti-hacking diagnostic (e.g., a held-out or adversarially chosen reward, or a human study), so this central claim remains under-evidenced relative to its prominence in the abstract and contribution list.

The 'functional equivalence to diffusion model RL' phrasing (Fig. 1 caption, abstract) overstates the analogy: weight-level RL changes the sampling distribution itself, whereas PromptLoop changes only the conditioning. The paper is more careful elsewhere ('structural analogy'), and the inconsistency between framing and mechanism should be reconciled.

The claim that at inference visual feedback is unnecessary (Sec. 3.3) sits awkwardly with the 'closed-loop' framing and with the ablation (Fig. 6) showing that visual feedback is indispensable during training. This important design decision is asserted rather than empirically ablated at inference time (e.g., inference with vs. without x̂_t).

Statistical reliability is unclear: several reported differences (e.g., HPSv2 deltas of ~0.01 in Table 2) are small, and no variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported for the main tables.

The generalization story is somewhat confounded: the policy is described as trained on a single 'vanilla diffusion model environment,' yet Table 2/3 report per-backbone rows for SD1.5, SDXL, and SDXL-turbo. It is not fully clear which rows correspond to a single jointly-trained policy versus per-model training, which matters for interpreting the generalization claims.

Some qualitative results (e.g., SD1.5+PromptLoop in Table 3 with negative ImageReward, and certain Fig. 11/13 examples) show that improvements are not uniform across prompts/backbones, but failure modes and prompt-level variance are not analyzed.

strengths: Clean and well-motivated MDP formulation that establishes a structural correspondence with Diffusion RL (Table 1, Fig. 3): the state (x_t, c_t, q, t) → action c_{t-1} mapping is sensible and gives the prompt-refinement framework a principled RL scaffold rather than an ad-hoc loop.

The plug-and-play design is genuinely practical: the sparse refinement set R bounds policy invocations, and the empirical finding that visual feedback is not needed at inference allows all refined prompts to be generated a priori, so the diffusion generation loop requires no modification. This is a meaningful engineering advantage over closed-loop alternatives.

Empirical breadth is strong for a single paper: three diffusion backbones (SD1.5, SDXL, SDXL-turbo), single- and composite-reward settings, orthogonality tests stacked on top of DDPO, Diffusion-DPO, ReFL, NPNet, and RePrompt, and cross-model generalization to backbones unseen in training (Tables 2 and 3, Figs. 4, 5, 11-14).

The ablation study (Table 4, Fig. 6) isolates each design choice cleanly: the untrained policy degrades performance, GRPO training recovers it, multiple within-trajectory refinements add further gains, and visual feedback raises the target reward without eroding other metrics.

The prompt-evolution analysis (Table 5, Appendix D.1) is an insightful emergent-behavior study, showing that the learned policy implicitly reproduces CFG-like schedules at the text level - early atmospheric descriptors, mid-trajectory concrete details, later refinement or collapse to prototypes. This is a nice interpretability contribution.

Reproducibility is above average: Algorithms 1 and 2, LoRA/GRPO hyperparameters (rank, lr, group size, KL coefficient), exact prompt templates (Figs. 7-10), reward implementations, and baseline checkpoints are all documented, with public code referenced for baselines.
weaknesses: Evaluation circularity and self-judging: ImageReward serves as both the training reward and a headline evaluation metric, and the VLLM Score is produced by Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct - the exact backbone used as the policy model. Improvements on these two columns are therefore partly expected by construction and do not constitute independent evidence of better alignment. The only fully external signals are HPSv2 and the aesthetic predictor, where the gains are real but smaller.

The central claim about mitigating reward hacking and over-optimization rests largely on qualitative examples (Fig. 4) plus the observation that non-target metrics do not degrade. No human study is provided, and no targeted experiment (e.g., reward-model ensembling, held-out reward functions, or measuring the gap between proxy reward and human judgment) directly tests the anti-hacking mechanism.

The claim that visual feedback is unnecessary at inference is asserted from an empirical observation but never quantitatively ablated. Fig. 6 contrasts training with and without visual feedback, not inference with and without latent states. If the claim holds, the deployed method reduces to timestep-conditioned prompt rewriting, which weakens the closed-loop framing and should be stated more carefully.

Novelty relative to RePrompt/OPT2I/RATTPO is incremental: the deltas are (i) consuming intermediate denoised latents as policy input during training and (ii) timestep conditioning. The 'functional equivalence to diffusion-model RL' is a conceptual analogy rather than a formal result, and the paper does not analyze under what conditions the analogy breaks down.

Composite-reward results are marginal and lack statistical support. In Table 3, GenEval moves 0.5445 → 0.5483 and 0.5431 → 0.5505, which is plausibly within run-to-run variance. No confidence intervals, seed variance, or significance tests appear anywhere in the paper, despite several claimed improvements being small.

Cost and scalability are under-reported. The policy MLLM must be co-resident with the diffusion model on 4×A100 80GB, and the per-refinement-step inference latency of the MLLM is never quantified, even though this is the main practical objection to the framework. The claimed efficiency gain over feed-forward prompt optimization is not measured.

Several implementation details that would matter for reproducing the claimed generalization are missing: the number of training prompts and optimization iterations, the sensitivity to N_R (trained with 2 refinement steps, sampled with 5), and how reward-name-only conditioning behaves on reward functions unseen during training.

strengths: Addresses a genuine limitation of prior prompt-refinement work: existing RL-based prompt methods (Promptist, RePrompt, PromptEnhancer) are largely feed-forward and apply a single refined prompt uniformly across the sampling trajectory, so embedding the policy inside the denoising loop is a reasonable and well-motivated direction.

The MDP formulation (state = (x_t, c_t, q, t), action = c_{t-1}, reward at x_0) is cleanly presented, and the explicit side-by-side comparison with weight-level Diffusion RL (Table 1, Fig. 3) makes the intended correspondence easy to follow.

Experiments are relatively broad: two diffusion backbones (SD1.5, SDXL) plus SDXL-turbo, several reward functions (ImageReward, aesthetics, compressibility/incompressibility, RePrompt-style composite), and composition/orthogonality tests on top of DDPO, Diffusion-DPO, ReFL, and NPNet. This is more evaluation breadth than many prompt-refinement papers provide.
Implementation details are reasonably complete (Qwen2.5-VL-3B policy, LoRA with r=16/alpha=64, GRPO settings, TRL/peft, A100 GPUs, prompt templates in the appendix), which aids reproducibility.
The appendix prompt-evolution analysis (Table 5) and the observation that learned prompt schedules resemble CFG scheduling is an interesting and interpretable qualitative finding.
weaknesses: The central claim is internally contradicted. The abstract, Fig. 1, and Fig. 3 present PromptLoop as a closed-loop method that uses latent feedback at each denoising step, yet Section 3.3 states that visual feedback 'is not strictly necessary at inference' and that refined prompts 'can be generated a priori.' If the loop is effectively open at inference, the headline novelty (step-wise latent feedback during sampling) collapses into a training-time-only construct, and the 'functional equivalence to diffusion model RL' (Fig. 1 caption) is not supported.

Evaluation is partially circular. ImageReward is used both as the training reward and as the primary evaluation metric, so the large ImageReward gains in Table 2 are largely expected; the more independent HPSv2 signal is nearly flat (e.g., 0.2805 -> 0.2807 on SDXL), which is consistent with reward-specific over-optimization rather than genuine alignment improvement. The VLLM Score is computed with Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct, i.e., the same model (family/size) used as the policy, which biases this metric toward the method's own prompt style.

The reward-hacking and human-preference claims, which are advertised as core contributions (contributions list, abstract (iv)), rest almost entirely on qualitative figures (Figs. 4, 5, 11-15) and on the same automatic proxies used for training. There is no human study, no adversarial or held-out reward audit, and no quantitative reward-hacking metric; the assertion that ReFL 'reward hacks' while PromptLoop does not is asserted rather than measured.

Novelty is incremental. RePrompt (Wu et al., 2025) already performs RL-based multi-turn prompt refinement, and the delta here is mainly (a) feeding intermediate denoised latents during training and (b) embedding refinement in one diffusion pass. Given the inference-time removal of feedback in (b), the remaining delta is modest and is not clearly separated from prior work in the experiments (e.g., Promptist is cited but not compared).

The ablation is ambiguous about training vs. inference feedback. Table 4 and Fig. 6 report 'w/o visual feedback' but never clarify whether feedback is removed at training, at inference, or both, which is exactly the distinction the paper's argument depends on. As written, the ablation cannot substantiate the claim that feedback is 'essential during training but unnecessary at inference.'

The 'plug-and-play' claim is under-supported. Section 3.3 itself notes the policy MLLM must be co-resident with the diffusion model or incur large transfer costs, and the sparse-refinement mitigation still requires multiple 3B-model invocations per image. No wall-clock, memory, or FLOPs comparison against baselines is provided, so the practical cost of the approach is not quantified.

The generalization/orthogonality evidence is narrower than claimed: the orthogonal-composition experiments apply the SD1.5-trained policy to SD1.5-based fine-tuned models, and the cross-backbone results (e.g., SDXL + PromptLoop) show only marginal cross-metric gains. The 'seamless generalization to unseen models' framing overstates what the tables show.

The 'structural/functional equivalence' language is used loosely. A discrete, high-level prompt action is not functionally equivalent to a continuous latent-noise action; the analogy is suggestive but the paper repeatedly blurs analogy and equivalence (e.g., Fig. 1 caption, Section 3.2), which risks over-claiming.

No significance testing is reported for the headline quantitative comparisons, and several reported deltas (HPSv2, Aesthetics) are within plausible noise, so the strength of the quantitative claims is unclear.

strengths: Clear, well-motivated problem formulation: the paper correctly identifies a real limitation of prior prompt-refinement methods (RePrompt, PromptEnhancer, RATT, etc.) — they apply a single refined prompt uniformly across all denoising timesteps and therefore do not exploit the sequential/trajectory structure that makes RL-based diffusion alignment effective. The proposed MDP (state = (x_t, c_t, q, t), action = refined prompt c_{t-1}) is a reasonable formalization of this gap.

Comprehensive empirical scope: two reward regimes (single-reward ImageReward and RePrompt-style composite reward), three diffusion backbones (SD1.5, SDXL, SDXL-turbo), and a broad baseline set (DDPO, ReFL, Diffusion-DPO, DanceGRPO, NPNet, Qwen2.5-VL-3B, GPT-5, RePrompt). The orthogonality experiments (applying PromptLoop on top of DDPO, ReFL, Diffusion-DPO, NPNet, DanceGRPO) are a particularly convincing way to show that the method is complementary rather than merely competitive.

Generalization demonstration is a genuine strength: the policy trained on diffusion models transfers zero-shot to unseen flow-matching models (SD3.5-large, FLUX.1-dev) with SNR-based timestep alignment (Table 6), and the plug-and-play design keeps the policy size fixed while diffusion backbones scale.

Well-designed ablations (Table 3, Fig. 6, Table 7) cleanly isolate the contributions of the policy model, GRPO training, multiple refinement steps, and training-time visual feedback, and the finding that visual feedback is essential during training but can be dropped at inference is a useful practical insight.
Runtime analysis (Table 4, Fig. 6) is honest and concrete: 15.00s → 18.43s with 5 refinement steps (1.23×), which supports the 'practically negligible overhead' claim rather than merely asserting it.

The prompt-evolution analysis (Appendix D, Table 5, Fig. 11, Fig. 12) is an interesting and somewhat unexpected finding — the learned policy recovers a CFG-like schedule (coarse/atmospheric descriptors early, concrete details at intermediate timesteps) without being explicitly instructed, and the token-length and semantic-drift analyses address legitimate practical concerns about prompt-based control.

The appendix is thorough: Algorithm 1/2, exact policy prompts (Figs. 7–10), implementation hyperparameters (LoRA rank, GRPO settings, batch/group sizes), and reward-model specifications. This materially aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Overclaiming of 'equivalence' to weight-level diffusion RL. The abstract and Fig. 1 caption use language such as 'functional equivalence to diffusion model RL' and 'structural equivalence to parameter-level fine-tuning,' while Fig. 3 and the main text soften this to 'structural analogy.' The diffusion parameters are frozen and the transition dynamics are those of the frozen sampler; the action space is text, not latents. This is an analogy, not an equivalence, and the stronger phrasing in the abstract/Fig. 1 should be toned down.

Evaluation is heavily reward-metric dependent. ImageReward is both the training reward (single-reward setting) and the headline evaluation metric, so the largest reported gains (e.g., Table 1) are partly circular. The independent metrics (HPSv2, aesthetics, MLLM score) move in the same direction but by very small margins — e.g., HPSv2 values across the entire SDXL block span roughly 0.268–0.286, with PromptLoop at 0.2807 vs. SDXL at 0.2805. No variance estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported, so it is unclear whether these differences exceed run-to-run noise.

No human study is conducted despite 'Human Preference' being plotted prominently in Fig. 2(b) and HPSv2 being used as a proxy. Given that the paper's central claims include 'mitigates reward hacking' and 'improves human preference,' an actual human preference evaluation (even a small one) would substantially strengthen the argument and is currently a notable omission.

The reward-hacking mitigation claim is supported mainly by qualitative observation (e.g., ReFL images in Fig. 4) rather than a quantitative measure of hacking (e.g., divergence between proxy reward and held-out human/LLM judgments, or an explicit over-optimization curve). The ablation 'visual feedback improves target reward without reducing other metrics' is suggestive but indirect.

Baseline fairness is uneven. RePrompt is re-implemented by stripping visual feedback and multi-turn refinement from PromptLoop, and Qwen2.5-VL-3B/GPT-5 are used 'without GRPO training,' so these are not the strongest versions of the compared methods. Some care is taken (Appendix C.4), but a reader cannot easily tell how much of the reported margin reflects the method versus the re-implementation.

There is an unresolved tension in the inference story: the method is framed as 'closed-loop latent feedback,' but the paper also states that at inference the policy can generate refinements a priori without access to intermediate visual states. If visual feedback is not needed at inference, the closed-loop/latent-feedback framing is diluted and the practical difference from a feed-forward refinement scheme narrows; this should be discussed more explicitly.

Composite-reward results on SD1.5 remain negative on ImageReward (−0.0375 for +PromptLoop vs. −0.1315 for +RePrompt), so the method improves but does not resolve the composite-reward setting on weaker backbones. The paper does not analyze why this regime is harder beyond a brief note about prompt length.

Minor presentation inconsistencies: 'MLLM policy' vs. 'policy MLLM' usage, Fig. 1 caption's 'functional equivalence' vs. the body's 'structural analogy,' and the fact that Fig. 1(b) shows the same seed/step grid but the accompanying description ('multiple timestep-aware prompt updates … yield stronger alignment') is not quantitatively tied to those images.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and elegant: reframing prompt refinement as a step-wise MDP that structurally mirrors Diffusion RL (state = latent + prompt + timestep, action = refined prompt) is a clean and original contribution that meaningfully departs from feed-forward prompt-optimization baselines.

The empirical evidence is broad and consistent. Table 1 and Table 6 show PromptLoop improving ImageReward, HPSv2, aesthetics, and MLLM score across SD1.5, SDXL, SDXL-turbo, FLUX.1-dev, and SD3.5-large, including zero-shot generalization to unseen flow-matching backbones.

The orthogonality claim is convincingly demonstrated: applying PromptLoop on top of DDPO, ReFL, Diffusion-DPO, NPNet, and DanceGRPO yields additional gains (Fig. 5, Fig. 16, Fig. 18), which supports the plug-and-play framing rather than merely beating a single baseline.

The ablation studies (Table 3, Fig. 6, Fig. 11, Fig. 12, Fig. 14, Table 7) are thorough, isolating the contribution of the policy model, GRPO training, multi-step refinement, and training-time visual feedback, and demonstrating that gains are not merely attributable to a stronger base MLLM (GPT-5/Qwen2.5-VL prompting remains far below PromptLoop).

The runtime analysis (Table 4) and the sparse refinement strategy address the obvious efficiency concern of invoking the policy at every denoising step, showing only a modest overhead (15s → 18.43s at 5 steps).

The appendix is unusually complete, including algorithms, prompt templates, reward model details, prompt-evolution analysis, and discussion of the emergent correspondence between RL-learned prompt schedules and CFG scheduling—an interesting scientific observation.
Qualitative results (Fig. 4, Fig. 5, Fig. 15-19) support the quantitative claims and specifically illustrate mitigation of reward hacking that is not captured by HPS/aesthetic metrics alone.
weaknesses: The 'structural analogy' to Diffusion RL is presented somewhat strongly (e.g., 'functional equivalence'), but it is a design inspiration rather than a formal equivalence; the gradient structure and learning signal differ from true parameter-level RL, and the paper could state this more carefully.

Evaluation partly relies on reward models (e.g., ImageReward) that are also used as the training signal, which raises a mild circularity concern for the primary metric; independent metrics (HPSv2, aesthetics, MLLM score) partially mitigate this but do not fully eliminate it.

Composite-reward results (Table 2) are weaker and less clear-cut than the single-reward setting—SD1.5 composite ImageReward remains negative (-0.0375) and GenEval gains over SDXL-turbo are marginal—so the claim of robust composite alignment is not as strongly supported.

Fairness of some baselines is debatable: comparing PromptLoop (trained MLLM policy) against GPT-5/Qwen2.5-VL used zero-shot (without GRPO) may not isolate the value of step-wise latent feedback from the value of task-specific RL training, even if Table 7 partly addresses this.

The paper does not report diversity/FID-style metrics, so it is unclear whether improved reward alignment degrades sample diversity or introduces distributional collapse—an important consideration for alignment methods.
Some qualitative outputs (e.g., composite-reward examples in Fig. 17) exhibit artifacts and off-target compositions, suggesting the method is not uniformly reliable across all prompts.

strengths: The core idea—training an MLLM policy with GRPO to emit timestep-conditioned prompt schedules for a frozen diffusion model, using the diffusion trajectory as the RL state during training—is a reasonable and non-trivial extension of feed-forward prompt rewriting such as RePrompt and PromptEnhancer. Conditioning the refined prompt on the timestep, rather than applying one refined prompt uniformly across all steps, is a defensible technical contribution.

The empirical coverage is broad: two reward settings (single and composite), three backbones (SD1.5, SDXL, SDXL-Turbo), three secondary metrics (HPSv2, Aesthetics, MLLM score), the GenEval object-centric benchmark, orthogonality experiments on top of DDPO/ReFL/Diffusion-DPO/NPNet/DanceGRPO, and zero-shot transfer to flow-matching models (FLUX.1-dev, SD3.5-large, Table 6).

The engineering analyses are genuinely useful: component ablation (Table 3), scaling with the number of refinement steps (Fig. 6), measured inference overhead (Table 4), prompt-length growth and semantic-drift quantification (Figs. 11–12), and the timestep-wise prompt-evolution study (Table 5) that connects the learned behavior to CFG scheduling intuition.

Reproducibility is above average for a submission of this scope: training and sampling procedures are given as explicit algorithms (Alg. 1–2), all policy/reward prompts are shown verbatim (Figs. 7–10), and implementation details (LoRA rank, learning rate, group size, precision, hardware) appear in Appendix C.1.

The finding that training-time visual feedback is what matters, permitting open-loop inference, is potentially interesting as an efficiency and generalization observation—provided it is properly validated and honestly framed (which, as noted below, it currently is not).
weaknesses: The headline contribution—step-wise closed-loop latent feedback—is disabled at inference time, which contradicts the abstract, title framing, and figures. Sec. 3.3 states that refined prompts 'can be generated a priori, allowing the diffusion process to proceed without interruptions,' and Appendix C.1 confirms that 'during sampling, we insert the built-in token <|image_pad|> as a placeholder to replace the visual feedback.' Yet the abstract claims the MLLM 'iteratively update[s] prompts based on intermediate latent states,' Fig. 1(a) advertises 'stepwise prompt refinement,' and Fig. 2(a) is titled 'Closed-loop prompt refinement framework' with x_t explicitly fed to the policy. As actually deployed, the method is a (q, t) -> c_t prompt-schedule generator, so the 'structural analogy' to diffusion RL in Fig. 3 does not hold at test time (the action no longer depends on the latent state). The paper never quantifies what is lost by removing inference-time feedback, nor does it reconcile this with the '+ visual feedback' row of Table 3, whose scope (training vs. inference) is never made explicit.

The claim of mitigating reward hacking/over-optimization is not supported by controlled evidence. There is no experiment tracking a held-out, non-optimized objective over the course of alignment (e.g., HPSv2 or GenEval versus optimization steps or KL). In the tables, gains are concentrated almost entirely in the directly optimized reward (ImageReward), while secondary metrics move within noise: SDXL -> +PromptLoop gives HPSv2 0.2805 -> 0.2807, and on the flow-matching models in Table 6 HPSv2 is literally unchanged (0.286 -> 0.286 and 0.288 -> 0.288). This is the signature of reward over-optimization, not its mitigation. The primary evidence for the claim is qualitative (Fig. 4, plus the remark that ReFL outputs 'resemble reward hacking from a human perspective'), with no annotation protocol, rater count, or agreement statistics.

Baselines are not faithfully implemented, which confounds the comparisons. Appendix C.4 states that 'RePrompt is implemented by removing visual feedback and multi-turn refinement from PromptLoop; reasoning is also omitted,' i.e., the RePrompt baseline is an ablation of the authors' own system and is weaker by construction. Likewise Qwen2.5-VL-3B and GPT-5 are run without any RL training yet are listed in Table 1 alongside trained methods as if they were comparable setups.

The 'structural equivalence to parameter-level tuning' framing is overstated. Eq. (6) is a generic MDP over prompts; the paper establishes an analogy table (Fig. 3), not equivalence, and offers no test of the asserted functional correspondence (e.g., whether the learned prompt schedule recovers the behavior of a reward-fine-tuned model).

The inference-overhead claims are inconsistent with the paper's own measurements. Table 4 shows 15.00 s -> 18.43 s at five refinement steps (+23%), and Sec. 3.3 concedes that the MLLM and diffusion model 'must be co-resident on the accelerator,' which 'significantly increases the memory costs.' Nevertheless the abstract calls the overhead 'practically negligible' and the introduction calls it 'minimal.' The stated mitigation (sparse refinement) reduces the number of MLLM calls but does nothing about the memory footprint, and the obvious two-pass alternative that the a-priori generation design enables (run the policy, free it, then sample) is never discussed.

Differences on secondary metrics are marginal and reported without uncertainty. No seeds, error bars, or significance tests appear in the main tables, yet differences as small as 0.0001–0.0004 on HPSv2 (Tables 1 and 6) are used to support the claim that the method 'consistently outperforms baselines across most evaluation metrics.'

Two design choices undercut the 'plug-and-play, general alignment' narrative. First, training and evaluating with the same reward (ImageReward) makes the headline metric a training objective. Second, the reward name is passed to the policy as a string (Appendix C.2), so the policy can learn reward-specific behavior, making this closer to reward-conditioned prompt search than a general alignment mechanism. Moreover, Table 7 shows performance is dominated by the initialization policy (Qwen3-VL-4B: 0.6922 vs Qwen2.5-VL-3B: 0.6320), so it is unclear how much of the gain is attributable to the proposed RL training versus the base MLLM; a strong untrained MLLM run with the same multi-step template is absent from the main tables.
The only human-preference evidence, the bar chart in Fig. 2(b), has an unlabeled axis and no sample size, annotation protocol, or rater statistics, and is not corroborated anywhere else in the paper.

Presentation problems that materially hinder assessment: Table 1's layout makes it difficult to determine which rows share a training setup; the 'MLM Score' header is used inconsistently with 'MLLM Score'; Fig. 2(a) and Sec. 3.3/Appendix C.1 describe incompatible inference procedures; and the description of Diffuson-DPO vs. Diffusion-DPO in Appendix A and the tables is inconsistent.
